query: For a high-entropy alloy coating system on a transition metal matrix, what is the relationship between ambient temperature and tribological performance? Please hypothesize the dominant mechanism linking thermal conditions to wear resistance and propose a boundary where performance degrades.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings on transition metal matrices, tribological performance exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with ambient temperature, characterized by an initial improvement due to the formation of a protective tribo-oxide layer, followed by a sharp degradation once the temperature exceeds the onset of significant matrix softening and oxide layer instability.
generation.material_initial_state: A dense, nanocrystalline or equiatomic high-entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 or CoCrFeMnNi) deposited on a transition metal substrate (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V or 316L Stainless Steel) via physical vapor deposition or laser cladding, exhibiting high hardness and a stable solid-solution structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Subject the coated system to reciprocating sliding wear tests under controlled ambient temperatures ranging from 25°C to 800°C in an air atmosphere, while maintaining constant normal load and sliding velocity.
generation.conditions: Atmospheric pressure, dry sliding conditions, constant sliding velocity (e.g., 0.5 m/s), constant normal load (e.g., 10 N), and temperature steps of 50°C increments.
generation.structural_mediator: The competition between the formation of a protective, self-healing tribo-oxide layer (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3) and the thermally activated softening of the HEA matrix via dislocation climb and cross-slip mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures (25°C–400°C), wear resistance improves or remains stable because the frictional heat promotes the rapid formation of a continuous, adherent oxide tribofilm that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and acts as a solid lubricant. As temperature increases beyond a critical threshold (T_crit), the HEA matrix undergoes significant thermal softening due to the reduction in Peierls stress and the activation of multiple slip systems, which lowers the yield strength faster than the oxide layer can reform or adhere. This leads to the breakdown of the tribofilm, increased adhesive wear, and plastic deformation of the substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coefficient of friction will decrease initially as temperature rises to ~400°C due to oxide lubrication, then increase sharply above T_crit. The specific wear rate will show a minimum at ~400°C and increase exponentially above T_crit, indicating a transition from oxidative wear to severe adhesive/abrasive wear.
generation.baseline: Room temperature (25°C) wear performance of the same HEA coating system, where wear is dominated by mild abrasive and adhesive mechanisms without significant thermal oxide formation.
generation.boundary: The performance degradation boundary is defined as the temperature T_crit where the yield strength of the HEA coating drops below the critical shear stress required to maintain the integrity of the tribo-oxide layer, typically predicted to occur between 500°C and 600°C for most Cr/Al-containing HEAs in air.
generation.uncertainty: The exact value of T_crit is uncertain and highly dependent on the specific elemental composition of the HEA (e.g., presence of refractory elements like W or Mo may raise T_crit) and the specific sliding velocity which determines the flash temperature at the asperity contacts versus the bulk ambient temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in-situ high-temperature tribological testing combined with real-time Raman spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor the phase composition of the tribofilm and the hardness of the coating surface simultaneously as temperature increases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the wear rate continues to decrease monotonically up to 800°C without a distinct minimum, or if the tribofilm remains stable and protective even when the bulk coating hardness has dropped by more than 50% due to thermal softening, indicating that the oxide layer alone is sufficient to prevent wear regardless of matrix softening.

In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
